paragraphs.context: When I did research for Thanksgiving on Thursday
paragraphs.mainIdea: The "first Thanksgiving" was really a harvest festival.
paragraphs.simple: The author learned something new: the 1621 meal of the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag was not a special day to say thank you. It was a three-day party to celebrate a good harvest. Later, in 1863, President Lincoln made the last Thursday in November America's Thanksgiving Day.

background.note: English people who sailed to America in 1620 on the ship Mayflower and started the town of Plymouth.
A Native American people who lived (and still live) in the south-east of New England. Say it wom-puh-NO-ag.
The 16th president of the USA (1861–1865).
An American holiday on the fourth Thursday of November. Families eat a big dinner, often turkey, and give thanks.

paragraphs.context: I love doing the research for Magic Tree
paragraphs.simple: The author loves doing research because she always learns something new. She hopes you will learn new things too when you visit the "first Thanksgiving" with Jack and Annie.

paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a
paragraphs.simple: One summer day a strange tree house suddenly appeared in the woods of Frog Creek.

background.note: Frog Creek is the made-up town where Jack and Annie live. Pennsylvania is a real state in the east of the USA.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie soon discovered that the tree
paragraphs.simple: The tree house can take Jack and Annie to the places in its books. They only point at a picture and wish. While they are away, no time passes at home.

paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house belongs to Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian from Camelot, King Arthur's kingdom. She travels through time and space and collects books.

background.note: King Arthur's castle and kingdom in old British stories.
A magic woman from the stories about King Arthur. In this series she is a kind librarian.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie have many exciting adventures helping
paragraphs.mainIdea: They will learn the art of magic.
paragraphs.simple: In books 25 to 28, Jack and Annie will learn about magic.

paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to check the woods.
paragraphs.simple: Annie stood at the door of Jack's bedroom and said they should go and look in the woods.

paragraphs.context: “I know,” said Annie. “But I have a
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the tree house is back and Morgan has sent a new rhyme.

paragraphs.context: “Okay, but we’ll have to be quick,” he
paragraphs.simple: Jack agreed but said they must be quick. He put his notebook and pencil in his backpack and went downstairs after her.

paragraphs.simple: Mom reminded them it was Thursday. They were going to Grandmother's house at nine o'clock.
paragraphs.tone: It is Thanksgiving Day, so the family is going to visit Grandmother.

paragraphs.context: They hurried out of their house. They ran
paragraphs.simple: They ran out of the house, across the yard, up the street and into the Frog Creek woods.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie ran through light and shadow
paragraphs.mainIdea: They stop at the tallest oak.
paragraphs.simple: They ran through sunny and dark places until they stopped under the tallest oak tree.

paragraphs.simple: Jack took hold of the rope ladder and climbed up. Annie was right behind him.

paragraphs.context: “Good, our gifts from our last trips are
paragraphs.simple: Annie was glad that the gifts from their last trips were still in the tree house.

paragraphs.context: She pointed to the scrolls from Shakespeare’s theater
paragraphs.simple: Annie pointed to the scrolls from Shakespeare's theater and the small stick from the gorillas.

background.note: In book 25, Jack and Annie went to William Shakespeare's theater in London (1601) and found the magic of the theater.
In book 26, they visited gorillas in an African cloud forest and found the magic of animals.

paragraphs.simple: Jack said these things show that they found the magic of the theater and the magic of animals.

paragraphs.context: “Look,” said Annie. She pointed to a book
paragraphs.simple: Annie pointed to a book in a dark corner. A piece of paper was coming out of it.

paragraphs.context: Good luck on your third journey to find
paragraphs.simple: Morgan wished them good luck on their third trip to find a special magic. A rhyme will show them the way.

paragraphs.simple: Jack asked who they would come together with.

paragraphs.simple: Annie held up the book. The picture showed a basket of corn on a wooden table. The title was A Feast to Remember.

paragraphs.context: “Hold on,” said Jack. “What kind of feast?
paragraphs.simple: Jack said, "Wait! What kind of feast? Where and when?"
paragraphs.tone: Jack always wants to know facts before he goes. Annie just goes.

paragraphs.context: But the wind had started to blow.
paragraphs.simple: But the wind had already started to blow.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. Bright, golden sunlight poured
paragraphs.simple: Jack opened his eyes. Bright golden sunlight came into the tree house. The air felt fresh and cool.

paragraphs.context: Annie was wearing a long dress, a white
paragraphs.simple: Annie had a long dress, a white cap and a cloth over the front of her dress.

paragraphs.context: Jack wore a jacket with a frilly collar.
paragraphs.simple: Jack had a jacket with a fancy collar, short pants, long socks, leather shoes and a hat. His backpack was now a leather bag.

paragraphs.simple: Annie said Jack looked like a Pilgrim. Jack said so did she, and they must be in the time of the Pilgrims.

paragraphs.tone: Red and yellow leaves tell us it is autumn.

paragraphs.context: In 1620, a group of 102 passengers sailed
paragraphs.simple: In 1620, 102 people sailed from England to America on the Mayflower. Many wanted to pray to God in their own way, not the king's way. Others wanted a new life. We call them all Pilgrims.

background.note: The ship that carried the Pilgrims across the Atlantic Ocean in 1620. The trip took 66 days.

paragraphs.context: The Pilgrims wanted to settle near New York.
paragraphs.simple: The Pilgrims wanted to live near New York, but a storm blew them north. They landed in a bay in what is now Massachusetts. John Smith had named it Plymouth six years before.

background.note: A state in the north-east of the USA. Its capital is Boston.
An English explorer. In 1614 he made a map of this coast and named it "New England".

paragraphs.simple: Annie knew that Plymouth is where the first Thanksgiving happened.

background.note: William Bradford, the leader of Plymouth Colony for over 30 years.
The soldier who led the Pilgrims' small army.

paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks Annie is crazy. The Pilgrims will not understand who they are, so they need a plan.

paragraphs.simple: Jack put his bag over his shoulder and hurried down the ladder after Annie.

paragraphs.simple: They tried to walk carefully, but the dry autumn leaves made loud sounds under their shoes.

paragraphs.simple: They walked noisily to a tree at the edge of the woods. Far away they saw a row of small log houses with high roofs made of dry grass.

paragraphs.context: The Pilgrims brought chickens, geese, goats, and sheep
paragraphs.simple: The Pilgrims brought animals and seeds from England. But they could not have stayed alive without Squanto, a Wampanoag man. He taught them how to grow corn.

background.note: A Wampanoag man (real name Tisquantum) who spoke English and helped the Pilgrims to live in America.

paragraphs.context: Annie was talking to a skinny yellow dog.
paragraphs.simple: Annie was talking to a thin yellow dog that was smelling a tree.

paragraphs.simple: Two Pilgrim men ran from the houses, and then more came. They all looked toward the barking dog.

paragraphs.simple: Jack shouted as he was pulled up into the air.

paragraphs.context: “I must have stepped into a hunting trap,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack said in a tight voice that he must have stepped into a trap for catching animals.

paragraphs.simple: Jack heard voices. Many people came around him and Annie, but he could not see them clearly.

paragraphs.simple: A big strong man sent the dog away and held Jack. Another man cut the rope with a knife. They put Jack down carefully.

paragraphs.context: Jack sat in the leaves, feeling dizzy. He
paragraphs.simple: Jack sat in the leaves. He felt dizzy. He took off the rope and rubbed his ankle.

paragraphs.simple: Jack put on his things. Now he could see about forty or fifty Pilgrims looking at them. Some children laughed.

paragraphs.simple: One man looked different. He had brown skin, a deer skin over his shoulder, and long black hair with a feather in it.

paragraphs.simple: Jack wondered if this man was Squanto, the Wampanoag man who helped the Pilgrims.

paragraphs.tone: The Pilgrims speak old English: "thou" = you, "art" = are.

paragraphs.context: “I’m Annie,” said Annie. “This is my brother
paragraphs.simple: Annie said who they were and said they were friendly.

background.note: The town and land the Pilgrims built in 1620. It was the second English colony in America.

paragraphs.tone: Funny: modern words like "wow", "nuts" and "oh, brother" sound strange to the Pilgrims.

paragraphs.simple: A young woman said she was Priscilla. She was about 17 or 18. She looked tired, and her eyes were sad.

background.note: Priscilla Mullins, a real Pilgrim. Her parents and brother died in the first winter.

parts.meaning: Our parents sent us here to ...

parts.text: —he remembered something from their research book—
parts.meaning: (he thought of a fact from the book)

parts.text: “to learn how to grow corn.”
parts.meaning: to learn how to grow corn.

sentences.grammar: Dashes show an action in the middle of speech. "Um" and "uh" show Jack is nervous and making up the story.

sentences.context: Now that he had started making up a story, he couldn’t back out.
sentences.simple: He had already started telling a story that was not true, so he could not stop now.
sentences.main: He couldn't back out.

parts.text: Now that he had started making up a story,
parts.meaning: Because he had already started inventing a story,

parts.text: he couldn’t back out.
parts.meaning: he could not stop.

sentences.grammar: "Now that ..." = "because ... now". "Start + -ing": he started making up.

sentences.context: We welcome all the small folk sent to us. Children are a gift from God—no matter where they come from.
sentences.simple: We are happy to have all the children who come to us. Children are a gift from God, wherever they come from.
sentences.main: Children are a gift from God.

parts.text: We welcome all the small folk
parts.meaning: We are happy to have all the children

parts.text: sent to us.
parts.meaning: who are sent to us.

parts.text: Children are a gift from God
parts.meaning: Children are a present from God

parts.text: —no matter where they come from.
parts.job: "No matter where" = it is not important where.
parts.meaning: wherever they come from.

sentences.grammar: "Sent to us" is short for "who are sent to us". "No matter where/what/who" = it does not matter where/what/who.

sentences.context: We invited Chief Massasoit and his men to our harvest feast. But we did not expect so many. We have not prepared enough food.
sentences.simple: We asked Chief Massasoit and his men to come to our feast, but we did not think so many would come. We have not made enough food.
sentences.main: We have not prepared enough food.

parts.text: We invited Chief Massasoit and his men to our harvest feast.
parts.meaning: We asked the chief and his men to come to our feast.

parts.text: But we did not expect so many.
parts.job: The problem. "Expect" = think something will happen.
parts.meaning: But we did not think so many would come.

parts.text: We have not prepared enough food.
parts.meaning: So we don't have enough food ready.

sentences.grammar: "Did not expect so many" = "did not expect so many people to come".

sentences.context: He showed them how to push the eels out of the wet sand with their bare feet, then grab them with their hands.
sentences.simple: He showed them how to push eels out of the sand with their feet and then catch them with their hands.
sentences.main: He showed them how to catch eels.

parts.text: He showed them how
parts.job: Main part. "How + to" = the way to.
parts.meaning: He taught them the way

parts.text: to push the eels out of the wet sand with their bare feet,
parts.meaning: to push the eels out of the sand with their feet with no shoes,

parts.text: then grab them with their hands.
parts.meaning: then catch them with their hands.

sentences.grammar: "Show someone how to do something" = teach them. "Then + verb" = the next step.

sentences.context: Quahog clams are hard-shell clams. They can live for sixty years or more. The oldest have been known to live for almost 100 years.
sentences.simple: Quahog clams have hard shells. They can live 60 years or more. Some old ones lived almost 100 years.
sentences.main: They can live for sixty years or more.

parts.text: Quahog clams are hard-shell clams.
parts.meaning: Quahogs are clams with hard shells.

parts.text: They can live for sixty years or more.
parts.meaning: They can live 60 years or longer.

parts.text: The oldest have been known to live for almost 100 years.
parts.job: Fact 3. "Have been known to" = people know that they did.
parts.meaning: We know some lived almost 100 years.

sentences.grammar: "Have been known to do" = it has really happened. "The oldest" = the oldest clams.

sentences.context: He hoped the governor and the captain wouldn’t ask him about home. Jack hid his face behind the fat pumpkin.
sentences.simple: Jack hoped the governor and the captain would not ask about his home, so he hid behind the big pumpkin.
sentences.main: Jack hid his face behind the pumpkin.

parts.text: He hoped
parts.meaning: He wished

parts.text: the governor and the captain wouldn’t ask him about home.
parts.job: What he hoped. "Wouldn't" = future in the past.
parts.meaning: the two leaders would not ask where he lived.

parts.text: Jack hid his face behind the fat pumpkin.
parts.meaning: So he put the big pumpkin in front of his face.

sentences.grammar: After a past verb like "hoped", we use "would" for the future: "He hoped they wouldn't ask."

sentences.context: The Pilgrims called leafy vegetables that grow above the ground herbs.
sentences.simple: The Pilgrims used the name "herbs" for vegetables with leaves that grow above the ground.
sentences.main: The Pilgrims called leafy vegetables herbs.

parts.text: The Pilgrims called
parts.job: "Call A B" = give A the name B.
parts.meaning: The Pilgrims gave the name

parts.text: leafy vegetables that grow above the ground
parts.meaning: vegetables with leaves that grow over the ground

parts.text: herbs.
parts.meaning: "herbs".

sentences.grammar: "Call + thing + name": "We call him Tom." Here the thing is long, so the name "herbs" comes at the very end.

sentences.context: But we never gave up hope. And now, God be praised, we have had a good harvest, and we have peace with our neighbors.
sentences.simple: But we always kept hoping. And now, thank God, we have a good harvest and peace with our neighbors.
sentences.main: We never gave up hope.

parts.text: But we never gave up hope.
parts.meaning: But we always kept hoping.

parts.text: And now, God be praised,
parts.meaning: And now, thank God,

parts.text: we have had a good harvest,
parts.meaning: we got a lot of food from our fields,

parts.text: and we have peace with our neighbors.
parts.meaning: and we are friends with the people near us.

sentences.grammar: "Give up" = stop. "God be praised" is an old wish: "Let God be praised."

sentences.context: Not only was she kind, but she was incredibly brave as well.
sentences.simple: She was kind, and she was also very, very brave.
sentences.main: She was kind and brave.

parts.text: Not only was she kind,
parts.job: Part 1. Note the order: "was she", not "she was".
parts.meaning: She was kind,

parts.text: but she was incredibly brave as well.
parts.meaning: and she was also very brave.

sentences.grammar: When a sentence starts with "Not only", the verb comes before the subject: "Not only was she kind, but ..."

sentences.context: The long guns are muskets, which are also called arms. So “exercising arms” means firing muskets!
sentences.simple: Muskets are long guns, and another name for guns is "arms". So "exercising arms" means shooting guns.
sentences.main: “Exercising arms” means firing muskets.

parts.text: The long guns are muskets,
parts.meaning: The long guns are called muskets,

parts.text: which are also called arms.
parts.meaning: and muskets have another name: arms.

parts.text: So “exercising arms” means firing muskets!
parts.meaning: So "exercise arms" = shoot guns!

sentences.grammar: ", which ..." adds more information about the word before it (muskets).

sentences.context: The Pilgrims had worked so hard to get their food. They had had such a terrible winter—especially Priscilla.
sentences.simple: The Pilgrims worked very hard for their food, and their winter was terrible, most of all for Priscilla.
sentences.main: They had had a terrible winter.

parts.text: The Pilgrims had worked so hard to get their food.
parts.meaning: The Pilgrims worked very hard for their food.

parts.text: They had had such a terrible winter
parts.meaning: Their winter was very bad

parts.text: —especially Priscilla.
parts.meaning: most of all for Priscilla.

sentences.grammar: "Had had" looks strange but is normal: the first "had" helps make the past perfect, the second is the verb "have".

sentences.context: And today, we give thanks for him, and for the peace we share with his people, and for all our great blessings.
sentences.simple: Today we say thank you for Squanto, for the peace with his people, and for all the good things we have.
sentences.main: We give thanks for him.

parts.text: And today, we give thanks
parts.meaning: Today we say thank you

parts.text: for him,
parts.meaning: for Squanto,

parts.text: and for the peace we share with his people,
parts.job: Thing 2. "We share" tells more about the peace.
parts.meaning: and for the peace between us and his people,

parts.text: and for all our great blessings.
parts.meaning: and for all the good things we have.

sentences.grammar: The word "for" is repeated three times to make a list of things they are thankful for.

sentences.context: Food really tastes good, he thought as he chewed, when you eat it outside, on a beautiful day, with lots of nice people.
sentences.simple: While he ate, Jack thought that food tastes very good when you eat it outside on a nice day with many nice people.
sentences.main: Food really tastes good.

parts.text: Food really tastes good,
parts.meaning: Food is really delicious

parts.text: he thought as he chewed,
parts.meaning: Jack thought while he ate

parts.text: when you eat it outside, on a beautiful day, with lots of nice people.
parts.job: When food tastes good: three things.
parts.meaning: if you eat outside, on a nice day, with friendly people.

sentences.grammar: "He thought" can come in the middle of a thought. "As" = while.

sentences.context: He feared that once they were alone, Squanto would figure out they’d never met before.
sentences.simple: He was afraid that when they were alone, Squanto would understand that they had never met.
sentences.main: He feared Squanto would figure out the truth.

parts.text: He feared that
parts.job: Main verb: what he was afraid of comes next.
parts.meaning: He was afraid that

parts.text: once they were alone,
parts.meaning: as soon as no one else was there,

parts.text: Squanto would figure out
parts.meaning: Squanto would understand

parts.text: they’d never met before.
parts.meaning: that they had never met before.

sentences.grammar: "Once" can mean "as soon as". "They'd never met" = "they had never met".

sentences.context: I remembered what it was like to be from a different world,” said Squanto. “Long ago, I lived with my people on this shore. But one day, men came in ships. They took me to Europe as a slave.
sentences.simple: Squanto said he remembered how it feels to come from a different world. Long ago, men came in ships and took him to Europe as a slave.
sentences.main: I remembered what it was like to be from a different world.

parts.text: I remembered what it was like
parts.job: "What it is like" = how it feels.
parts.meaning: I remembered how it felt

parts.text: to be from a different world,
parts.meaning: to come from a different place,

parts.text: ” said Squanto. “
parts.meaning: (Squanto is talking)

parts.text: Long ago, I lived with my people on this shore.
parts.meaning: Long ago, I lived here with my people.

parts.text: But one day, men came in ships. They took me to Europe as a slave.
parts.meaning: But men came in ships and took me to Europe and made me a slave.

sentences.grammar: "What is it like to ...?" = "How does it feel to ...?"

sentences.context: But when Squanto returned to Plymouth in 1619 after being kidnapped as a slave, he discovered that all his people had died in a plague in 1617.
sentences.simple: Squanto had been taken away as a slave. When he came back to Plymouth in 1619, he found that all his people had died of an illness in 1617.
sentences.main: He discovered that all his people had died.

parts.text: But when Squanto returned to Plymouth in 1619
parts.meaning: When Squanto came back in 1619

parts.text: after being kidnapped as a slave,
parts.job: "After + being + past participle" = after someone did this to him.
parts.meaning: after people took him away as a slave,

parts.text: he discovered that
parts.meaning: he found out that

parts.text: all his people had died in a plague in 1617.
parts.meaning: all his people died of a terrible illness in 1617.

sentences.grammar: "After being kidnapped" = after he was kidnapped (passive). "Had died" happened before "discovered".

put on a play.example: My class put on a play about the first Thanksgiving.

look up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

never mind.meaning: Don't worry about it; it is not important.
never mind.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

keep an eye on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

show off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.
